name: Amy Carmichael
title: Amy Carmichael: a family of care at Dohnavur
description: Amy Carmichael, her Indian co-workers and Dohnavur from 1901 onward: a story of child protection checked against institutional and academic sources.

sections.heading: Service took the shape of a home
paragraphs: Amy Carmichael arrived in South India in 1895. She had served in Japan before. She learned Tamil and worked alongside Indian Christian women. Jocelyn Murray’s academic biography places her work within a network that included Thomas Walker, his family and local co-workers.

In 1901, Carmichael and her companions settled in Dohnavur. The care of vulnerable children came to hold a central place in her work. The Dohnavur Fellowship recalls the growth of homes, schools and other services. That history was built by a community, and not only by the woman many called Amma, mother.

sections.heading: A ministry that continued through illness
paragraphs: A fall in 1931 and the health problems that followed severely limited her mobility. Carmichael kept writing and preparing others to take on responsibilities. The Boston University overview documents that change in her activity: illness changed the way she served during the years she had left.

The sources describe rescues of children exposed to exploitation and danger. Telling that context requires precision and respect for the people who were cared for. Their lives are not mere illustrations in a European biography. The protection and future of the children are the heart of the work that the sources allow us to recognize.

reflection: Mark 10:13–16 shows Jesus welcoming children and correcting those who kept them from coming to him. That passage guides a reflection on the worth of each child, above any usefulness his or her story may have for an adult or an organization. Caring requires listening and protecting their dignity.

The Dohnavur story invites us to think about care that lasts: education, health, companionship and safety. It also reminds us that an illness can change a person’s work without canceling every possibility of service. A mature community shares responsibilities and allows others to carry on a task, without making its identity depend on a single name.
review_note: The sources differ on the form of her name and her birthplace; the name Amy Carmichael is used without forcing those details. Practices are not generalized to all of India.
source_labels: Jocelyn Murray. “Carmichael, Amy Beatrice,” Biographical Dictionary of Christian Missions, ed. Gerald H. Anderson (1998), p. 116; Boston University, History of Missiology. The page also contains an overview by Lisa Beth White.
